newsitem.title: POLAND: RISING FLOOD SWAMPS PARTS OF POLISH CITY WROCLAW.
newsitem.headline: RISING FLOOD SWAMPS PARTS OF POLISH CITY WROCLAW.

text.p: A surge of water raging north along the Odra River from flooded southern Poland swamped suburbs of Wroclaw on Saturday while volunteers built sandbag walls in a bid to save the historic city's centre.
"The situation is getting worse, there is still a threat to the city and its most precious historic area," Ludwik Ryng, a spokesman for the provincial governor, told Reuters.
"We are waiting for the crisis to break one way or the other during the night....we are optimistic -- the way Wroclaw people mobilised themselves is most impressive," he said.
PAP news agency reported that governor Bogdan Zdrojewski said he planned to blast a gap in flood walls south of Wroclaw to free water into the countryside and rescue the city centre.

But it said he refused to tell reporters where or when this would happen because of rural residents determined to stop their homes and farms being sacrificed. Zdrojewski said people flooded out due to the measure would get priority for aid.
The floods, caused by downpours earlier this week, have taken at least 26 lives, police said.
Many thousands of people have been evacuated from scores of towns and hundreds of villages, leaving eerily deserted communities where streets had turned into deep rushing rivers.
Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz has called the flooding the region's worst natural disaster in centuries.

Reuter photographer Pawel Kopczynski said teams of emergency services and volunteers were frantically laying sandbags to protect the low-lying island where some of Wroclaw's most valuable old buildings stand.
Priceless old books and archives in the university library there were being hastily safeguarded.
In outer districts, water poured over defences and rose with a speed that astonished residents as they fled to upper stories to await rescue.
By evening Kopczynski reported similar scenes in some inner city streets of Wroclaw, which until borders changed in 1945 was the German city Breslau.
The city of Opole, further south, gave a foretaste on Friday of the fate that could await the 650,000 people in Wroclaw, when the waters coursed right into the centre.

Many citizens and villagers had not left their homes in advance, for fear of looters or from a desire to stay with everything they held dear. Some had to be coaxed by rescuers into boats after the floods arrived.
By Friday 3,500 sq km (2,170 sq miles) of Poland lay under water due to the floods which also ravaged the Czech Republic.
PAP quoted Interior Minister Leszek Miller as saying that a government reconstruction plan for the affected regions, now being drafted, would cost at least $1 billion.
Miller said Poland would have to amend this year's budget, make provisions in the 1998 one and borrow from the World Bank or other international institutions.

Prime Minister Cimoszewicz had said on Friday that changing the current budget, which would mean recalling parliament from recess, was not necessary for now as the government was able to raise $200 million for relief and reconstruction.
Even as waters receded in southern areas and evacuees returned to devastation, dead animals and the risk of disease, the surge advanced mercilessly along the Odra and the Wisla.
Warsaw declared a flood alert although the Wisla tide was not expected to spill over when it hit the capital on Monday.

In neighbouring Germany, Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Bonn had made 400,000 marks ($224,000) available to help Poland and a convoy was setting out to take emergency equipment. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
